claims.claim: **Newborn screening for PKU should be a national requirement;** treat as soon as possible, ideally before 10 days of age.
claims.source_text: NBS for PKU should be considered a national requirement. Early detection is the prerequisite of early treatment and is cost effective. … Treatment should start as soon as possible, ideally before 10 days of age.

claims.claim: **Screen immigrant or refugee children younger than 6 years**, and test anyone unscreened with intellectual disability or neurological deficit, with or without behavioural or psychiatric problems.
claims.source_text: As a minimum, routine screening for PKU is strongly recommended for immigrant or refugee children younger than 6 years and selective (based upon specific clinical presentations) at any age. … Intellectual disability and/or neurological deficits with or without behavioural and psychiatric problems in unscreened children and adults should initiate diagnostic tests for PKU.

claims.claim: **Exclude BH4 defects and DNAJC12 deficiency in every hyperphenylalaninaemia**, and genotype the patient.
claims.source_text: In the differential diagnosis of all HPA, defects in BH4 metabolism and DNAJC12 deficiency should be excluded. … Patient genotyping is recommended as it is necessary to distinguish PAH deficiency from DNAJC12-deficiency. It may also help to predict sapropterin-responsiveness and assist in defining the metabolic phenotype.

claims.claim: **Treat every child whose untreated blood Phe is 360 μmol/L or more.** Below 360 μmol/L no treatment is needed, but keep monitoring Phe until at least 6 years of age.
claims.source_text: No treatment is recommended when untreated blood Phe levels are <360 μmol/L. Monitoring of blood Phe (at a lower frequency#) until a minimum of 6 years of age is recommended to determine if levels rise above 360 μmol/L. … In all children with untreated blood Phe levels ≥360 μmol/L treatment should be initiated.

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Target blood Phe:** 120–360 μmol/L up to age 12 years; 120–600 μmol/L from 12 to 18 years and in adults over 18; 120–360 μmol/L in pregnancy.
claims.source_text: In treated PKU patients up to the age of 12 years, the recommended therapeutic target Phe levels are 120-360 μmol/L … In treated PKU patients aged 12-18 years, the recommended therapeutic target Phe levels are 120-600 μmol/L. … In treated PKU patients aged >18 years, the suggested recommended therapeutic target Phe levels are 120-600 μmol/L. … In pregnancy, the recommended therapeutic target Phe levels are 120-360 μmol/L.

claims.claim: **Lifelong follow-up in a specialist metabolic centre for everyone with PKU**, including adults off Phe-lowering treatment, with access to a metabolic physician, dietitian and (neuro)psychologist.
claims.source_text: Lifelong follow-up in a specialist metabolic centre is recommended for any individual with PKU, including adults not on Phe lowering treatment. … All patients with PKU should have access to a metabolic physician, dietician and (neuro)psychologist

claims.claim: 🇦🇺 **Australasian targets (ASIEM):** keep Phe at 120–360 µmol/L until 12 years of age. Beyond 12, some patients may reasonably make an informed choice to run above 360 µmol/L, on an individual target, bearing in mind that lower levels tend to give better short- and long-term outcomes. ASIEM notes that the US guideline holds 120–360 µmol/L for life, while the European one (2017) accepts up to 600 µmol/L after 12.

claims.claim: 🇦🇺 **Clinic review (ASIEM):** in a multidisciplinary metabolic clinic, in person or by teleconference, at least 3-monthly through the first year of life, 6-monthly through childhood and yearly in adulthood. For children, the team brings together a physician, nurse, dietitian, psychologist and psychosocial worker experienced in PKU.

claims.claim: 🇦🇺 **Transition (ASIEM):** raise the move to adult care when the young person enters high school and revisit it every year; where no specialist adult service exists, the treating physician should find a suitable one before high school ends.

Phe/Tyr ratio As reported in the first European PKU guidelines, Phe/Tyr ratio has been correlated to the patient outcome and, on occasion, even to a greater extent than blood Phe control [6]. Sharman et al. reported a significant correlation between lifetime blood Tyr and lifetime Phe/Tyr ratio and Global Executive Composite of the BRIEF (r = - 0.546, p = .027 and r = 0.478, p = .049 respectively) in 13 children with PKU (mean age 13.95 ± 1.8 years), whereas this correlation was not present for lifetime Phe [97]. McGinnity et al. investigated the relationship between markers and cerebral glucose metabolism in 8 PKU and 3 HPA adults with memory problems. They reported that 8 of 11 patients had cortical deficits of cerebral glucose metabolism, and both mean, and SD historical Phe/Tyr ratio was more indicative than absolute blood Phe levels [77]. Blood Tyr has a wide diurnal variation associated with Phe-free/low Phe protein substitute supplemented with Tyr. A reliable Phe/Tyr ratio should be measured after an overnight fast [6]. Furthermore, the blood Phe/Tyr ratio is difficult to use in clinical practice, similar to Phe variation, as there is no clear recommended target range. Recommendation 19 Phe variation and Phe/Tyr ratio are not recommended as biomarkers for routine care. Level of evidence: low (C) Strength of recommendation: strong Expert opinion: completely agree (75 %), mostly agree (25 %), partially agree (0 %), mostly disagree (0 %), completely disagree (0 %) 7.2. Frequency of blood spot monitoring and outpatient clinic visits 7.2.1. Time to receipt of laboratory results Blood Phe is usually monitored by home blood sampling or in outpatient clinics. The primary method for monitoring involves patients/family caregivers sending blood Phe samples via postal services to the laboratory for analysis and timely reporting of the blood results to the patients/family caregivers is essential. As postal routines in countries differ, and some countries are dependent on plasma samples only, the recommendation focuses on the time between receiving the sample in the laboratory and reporting the result to the patients/caregivers in a routine situation. This should be a maximum of 2 working days. This is particularly relevant for pregnant women and children. However, even for adults a short roundabout time can serve as a motivating factor for sending in blood samples. PKU teams may need to instruct patients to send their samples on specific days if laboratories measure samples only once weekly. Consideration can be given to centralizing Phe measurements to a smaller number of laboratories to minimize between-laboratory variation [91]. 7.1.4. Other metabolic biomarkers Recent studies have evaluated other potential markers such as large neutral amino acids, neurotransmitter metabolites such as homovanillic acid [98], 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid [98], melatonin [99] and prolactin [100], and potential new biomarkers detected by untargeted metabolomics [101,102]. However, the clinical relevance of these novel markers is unknown. Recommendation 17 Blood Phe (either DBS and/or plasma) should be measured to monitor metabolic control, as this is the most clinically relevant biomarker. Level of evidence: moderate (B) Strength of recommendation: strong Expert opinion: completely agree (100 %), mostly agree (0 %), partially agree (0 %), mostly disagree (0 %), completely disagree (0 %) Recommendation 20* The time between receipt of a blood Phe sample by the laboratory and the patient/ caregivers receiving the result should be a maximum of 2 working days. Recommendation 18** Considering the necessity for frequent follow-up and immediate clinical care, analyses of DBS by MS/MS should be used in PKU monitoring on condition that: Level of evidence: expert opinion Strength of recommendation: strong Expert opinion: completely agree (65 %), mostly agree (35 %), partially agree (0 %), mostly disagree (0 %), completely disagree (0 %) • adequate sample quality is assured by regular training of patients and caregivers • the accuracy of the results is assured by the laboratory through accredited/certified pre-analytical and analytical procedures. Follow-up of patients with untreated Phe >360 μmol/L A minimum frequency of blood Phe measurements and outpatient clinic visits is suggested per age group. Newly diagnosed infants and women during the preconception period and pregnancy may require more frequent (at least once weekly) contact with the metabolic team to provide education, reassurance and close support to patients/family caregivers. As appropriate, contact may be in person, by telephone or by video consultation. Video consultations do have limitations and can only partly replace some outpatient visits, but are useful for patient education and may be helpful if patients are logistically unable to attend a clinic in person [103]. among centres. Of course, in these patients, there is a risk of Phe levels being marginally above 360 μmol/L. Since we aim for Phe levels <360 μmol/L preconceptionally and during pregnancy, it is essential to keep female patients in follow-up, in contrast to male patients. Patients with milder phenotypes are commonly responsive to sapropterin treatment and/or tolerate more natural protein, although heterogeneity exists between patients. Children on sapropterin treatment, with stable blood Phe levels towards the lower end of the range (e. g. < 240 umol/L) may require less frequent-follow up than those with Phe towards the upper end (e.g. > 300 umol L). The target Phe level for patients ≥12 years of age is 120-600 μmol/L, meaning that some patients might not require any treatment ≥12 years. When women are planning pregnancy, their blood Phe levels may need to be lowered (120-360 μmol/L), so females remain in regular follow up. Metabolic centre and team # to discuss issues such as the maternal PKU syndrome, management of nausea and vomiting of pregnancy, genetic counselling, and follow-up of the child after delivery All patients should be treated in a specialized metabolic centre with a specialized metabolic laboratory. The absolute minimum of health professionals within the metabolic team should be a metabolic physician and a dietician with experience in IMD. Access to a (neuro)psychologist and/or social worker is strongly recommended to support patients with acceptance of their disorder, treatment and for neurocognitive assessments [6]. A neuropsychologist often performs neurocognitive assessments, while a clinical psychologist focuses on assessing and helping patients with emotional or mental difficulties throughout life. Access to both is recommended. Level of evidence: expert opinion Strength of recommendation: conditional Expert opinion: completely agree (75 %), mostly agree (20 %), partially agree (5 %), mostly disagree (0 %), completely disagree (0 %) It is important that blood Phe samples are collected under the same conditions and at the same time of the day in order to compare the results. Although it was always assumed that fasting Phe levels were the highest throughout the day, recent literature shows that this is not necessarily the case [104,105]. Several studies confirm earlier research [6] that unevenly divided intake of natural protein does not significantly influence Phe fluctuation during the day but that unevenly divided intake of protein substitutes does [104,105]. Blood Tyr levels are known to fluctuate widely (up to 300 %) during the day which could be explained by the ingestion of the Tyr-enriched protein substitute [6,105]. To estimate reliable Tyr levels, blood samples should be collected in the morning after fasting overnight. Centres of excellence In Europe, centres of excellence for metabolic diseases, including PKU, have been established in some countries. The decision to endorse a centre as an expert facility for PKU or another rare disease (prevalence of <1:2000 people) lies with national governments/health services. This process differs across countries. In some countries, governments have designated all centres treating metabolic diseases as expert facilities for PKU, while in other countries only a few metabolic centres have been endorsed as centres of expertise for PKU. 11 A.M.J. van Wegberg et al. Molecular Genetics and Metabolism 145 (2025) 109125 The aim is to ensure every patient with any rare disease is connected to a centre of excellence. This connection allows for the collection and sharing of knowledge, thereby ensuring optimal care for patients. The list of European expertise centers for rare diseases, and thereby for PKU can be found at Orphanet (https:www.orpha.net). Centres officially endorsed by their governments for a centre of excellence can be a member of MetabERN (the European Reference Network for Metabolic Diseases). The primary goal of ERNs is to identify where in Europe highlevel PKU care can be sought, especially in countries or regions where PKU care is not well established. It is based on the principle that any patient with a rare disease within Europe should have free access to excellent care. inexperience with maternal PKU care. Specific adult services may not be available in some countries or may be geographically distant from patients [115,116]. Video consultations may help. If a pediatric clinic is still involved, it should be acknowledged that adults should be managed differently. Recommendation 25* Young adults should be transferred from pediatric services to a specialized adult metabolic team to ensure lifelong specialized follow-up. Transition should be performed in a structured manner. This process should ideally be started in early adolescence. Level of evidence: low (C) Strength of recommendation: strong Expert opinion: completely agree (80 %), mostly agree (20 %), partially agree (0 %), mostly disagree (0 %), completely disagree (0 %) 7.4. Transition and patients lost to follow-up Recommendation 26** Clinicians should be aware of the reasons for disengagement from the metabolic clinic and adult patients should be offered an open invitation to return to the clinic if they request further follow up. Transition is a continuous process by which the primary responsibility for treatment is forwarded from parent/family caregiver to the patient, and from pediatric to adult medical services. This is a longterm process in which children gradually learn about their condition and treatment from an early age and then start to take the lead in their care. At the same time, parents should be guided to step down from their leading and controlling role. Acknowledging that this is a very individual process, some patients will have completed this process before the age of 18 years, while others continue to be supported by their parents/caregivers well into young adulthood. During adolescence and/ or young adulthood, it is not uncommon for patients to struggle with maintaining their treatment regimen. The transition process therefore needs to be well planned and individualized with involvement of both patient and parents/caregivers. There are various toolkits available that can help guide this process like the "Ready Steady Go" programme [106]. All patients should be transferred from pediatric to adult care. The timing of this transfer commonly occurs between 16 and 18 years of age, although some flexibility is required depending on the maturity and circumstances of the patient. Biasucci et al. recently proposed a pathway to set up a successful PKU transition process [107]. Ernst et al. reported in a group of patients 2 years after participating in an education programme, a positive influence on self-efficacy and an active role in their own treatment [108]. Peres et al. reported that 2 years after transfer, patient attendance remained high and blood Phe levels remained stable [109]. Mutze et al. reported that of 96 patients who were transferred to an adult team in the last 10 years, 81 % still maintained contact with their medical/dietetic teams and that metabolic control was stable [110]. In addition, most patients (83 %) were satisfied with the transition process and adult care [110]. In contrast, in Austria, Beghini et al. identified a high number of patients "lost to follow-up" (LTFU) using the NBS data between 1966 and 2000 and follow-up data of the metabolic centres. As many as 177 of 279 patients were LTFU, defined as no recorded contact and no blood Phe measurement for 2 years [111]. The impact of neuropsychological and neurocognitive deficits on patient ability and organization skills, inadequate knowledge of treatment recommendations, lack of insurance coverage, inadequate transition to adult care and fear can also contribute to LTFU [112-114]. A focus group of 8 PKU patients who were LTFU for over 2 years reported that they felt unprepared to continue treatment as adults and feared being judged by clinicians for allowing treatment to lapse [114]. Clinicians should be aware of the reasons for disengagement and contact patients to notify them that they can always return to the clinic regardless of their treatment status. If possible, without a new clinician referral. Neurocognitive functioning Cognitive impairment should be monitored in PKU. Neuropsychological assessment is important to evaluate the effects of new treatments and possible changes occurring across the lifespan. To monitor cognition in clinical practice, there is a need to establish which measures are most appropriate for the PKU population. In children with PKU, studies have frequently shown impairment compared to controls in working memory, inhibitory control, sustained attention, and abstract reasoning and the level of impairment has been associated with blood Phe [6,62,117]. In early-treated adults with PKU, meta-analysis has shown that reasoning, visual-spatial attention speed, sustained attention, visuo-motor control, and flexibility are the most strongly affected cognitive functions [3]. Studies from the literature have used different tasks to evaluate cognitive impairment in PKU, with multiple options being available to assess a given cognitive function. Results have been variable across studies, but there are also enough communalities to allow us to put forward some suggestions of the type of tasks to include in an assessment which should be sensitive to PKU impairment and to the level of metabolic control. Cognitive tasks generally require a combination of skills, even when they are categorized, for convenience, under a single label. In PKU, the tasks that are most sensitive require a combination of executive functions, processing speed, and fluid (processing new information) rather than crystallized knowledge (accumulated knowledge), particularly in adults. Examples include: • Digit symbol coding, trial-making test B-A [69,75], assessing flexibility/planning, visuo-motor coordination, and processing speed; • Visual search tasks assessing flexibility/planning, working memory, visuo-spatial attention, and processing speed: [66,69]; • Verbal fluency tasks assessing flexibility/planning and lexical retrieval; • Dot tasks [66,76], rapid visual information processing task (RIVP) [69] and continuous performance test [62], assessing sustained attention • Go-no-go tasks assessing inhibitory control, processing speed: [117,118]; 12 A.M.J. van Wegberg et al. Psychosocial functioning Time (minutes) Health-related quality of life (HRQoL) has been widely researched. Results of generic HRQoL questionnaires completed by patients/family caregivers indicate a good quality of life. The PKU-specific QoL-questionnaire (developed with assistance from industry) can address the specific problems encountered in PKU [6] and is a valid tool to evaluate before and after an intervention [121]. Unfortunately, this questionnaire is not free to access. A PKU impact score (PKU SSIS) has also been developed (by industry) to address the burden of illness [122]. Recent papers have confirmed an overall normal HRQoL in patients with PKU [75,123,124]. Aitkenhead et al. reported no difference between 149 adults with PKU and 74 controls in educational, occupational, quality of life or emotional outcomes, or on a measure of family functioning, and showed only minor differences in relationship style [75]. Huijbregts et al. however demonstrated adults had lower scores on cognition and domains of depressive mood and anger. A negative association with lifetime Phe was demonstrated for sleep, pain, anger, and sexuality [124]. Vieira et al. reported a low HRQoL in a cohort of Brazilian early treated PKU children, probably resulting from the harmful intellectual consequences due to poor adherence and challenges within the healthcare system [125]. Using the PKU-specific QoL Questionnaire, excellent HRQoL was demonstrated in adolescents and adults, but suboptimal metabolic control was negatively associated with HRQoL [126,127]. Anxiety about blood Phe levels (during pregnancy) received the highest scores in 21 Turkish adults [128]. Using Time Trade- Trade-Off and Discrete Choice Experiment surveys, dietary Phe restriction and symptoms negatively associated with HRQoL [129]. To conclude, although the overall HRQoL is normal in patients with PKU, certain domains of wellbeing may be impacted. 5 5 5 5 5 5 7 • Pegboard tasks, motor screening task, motor performance tasks [69,119,120] assessing visuo-motor control:; • California verbal learning task (CVLT) [75,83], rey auditory verbal learning test (RAVLT) [74], assessing verbal memory and learning: Some tasks where no impairment is expected could be included as control tasks to better evaluate specific effects of changes in metabolic control (e.g., tests examining vocabulary and spelling in adults). The following neuropsychological assessment for patients is suggested although the limited evidence on which this is based is acknowledged (Table 3). For the frequency of assessment, recommendations are based on knowledge from developmental psychology of sensitive windows of cognitive and social development and clinical practice in PKU care. It is recommended to offer neurocognitive assessment as a minimum: 1) at the start of formal education around 4-6 years to ensure that the child is ready for school and there are no issues that need attention, 2) at 12 years of age as target blood Phe levels change, adherence to dietary treatment may decline, and there is often a transition to a new education environment, 3) at 18(- 20) years when there will be increasing independence and a transfer to adult clinical services, 4) every (5-)10 years thereafter to ensure that cognition is stable and to provide a reference point in case of any subjective cognitive change with aging. Recommendation 28* Health-Related Quality of Life, psychosocial functioning and general wellbeing should be discussed at least annually in the outpatient clinic. For all patients, anxiety regarding blood levels and guilt about non-adherence should be discussed. The use of a questionnaire may be considered to support this. Testing should include IQ and the domains executive functioning (especially reasoning, cognitive flexibility and working memory) and sustained attention. Tests should preferably involve visuo-spatial stimuli and a processing speed component. Tasks tapping a combination of functions would be most sensitive. Mental health The impact of early treated PKU on mental health is most likely to be multifactorial, associated with the experience of a long-term health condition, elevated blood Phe associated with executive function deficits, and individual and family coping strategies, as demonstrated in earlier, mainly pediatric, studies [6]. Mental health is a state of mental well-being that enables people to cope with the stresses of life, realize their abilities, learn well and work satisfactorily, build relationships and contribute to their community (https://www.who.int/news-room/fact -sheets/detail/mental-health-strengthening-our-response). Mental health conditions include mood disorders, anxiety disorders, personality disorders and psychotic disorders, however mental health is more than the absence of mental disorders. (https://www.who.int/news-room/ fact-sheets/detail/mental-health-strengthening-our-response). Internalizing symptoms such as anxiety, withdrawal, low mood, depression, and distress have also been reported in some adult patients [131-134]. Currently it is not fully understood to what extent factors such as disease burden and increased blood Phe levels influence mental health. Some studies report a relationship with concurrent blood Phe [78,83], blood Phe of the preceding two years [81,131], lifetime blood Phe [135] or childhood blood Phe [66,136], while other studies reported no relationship between blood Phe levels and internalizing problems [134]. Anxiety may be associated with a controlling style of parenting during childhood as authors report higher anxiety scores in patients with the lowest blood Phe levels in childhood [75,86]. As reported in the first European PKU guidelines, an intervention Phe loading study showed worse mood with high Phe levels and an intervention sapropterin study, reported improved ADHD symptoms with lower blood Phe levels [6]. A recent intervention study reported improvement on depression scales with better dietary control, but without blood Phe correlation [79]. In trials where blood Phe levels were decreased using pegvaliase, no relationship between Profile of Mood States (POMS) scores and Phe was found [137]. Regardless of the cause of mental health symptoms, it is clear that they are present in a subset of patients with PKU and therefore assessment and support should be part of every routine clinic consultation, especially from adolescence. alterations is further supported by white matter signal improvement following lowering of blood Phe [6,138]. More recent MRI studies also pointed to the involvement of GM in adult early treated PKU patients. Those studies reported decreased GM volume [143,144] and a correlation between the regional pattern of grey matter atrophy and the profile of serotonin and dopamine metabolite depletion in CSF [98]. As for WM abnormalities, the clinical impact of these alterations is not clear. Recommendation 30 Neuroimaging should not be included among the tools for routine monitoring of the disease in healthy individuals with early treated PKU but should be reserved for patients exhibiting an unexpected clinical course and/or unexpected neurological deficits or for research purposes. Other organs Recent data suggest that involvement of other organs like eye, heart and kidney might be included in the spectrum of PKU involvement. 7.9.1. Eye In PKU, there are some studies indicating the possibility of loss of vision that may have a relation with earlier studies that highlighted decreased visual evoked potential (VEP) latencies in early (as well as late) treated patients with PKU. It was suggested that long chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (LC-PUFA) may be influential as both eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) status and VEP latencies improved in PKU patients receiving LC-PUFA supplementation [145-147]. Gramer et al. studied LC-PUFA status and the dopamine hypothesis (i.e. increased blood Phe may cause decreased dopamine levels in the brain and eye associated with inadequate Tyr in the central nervous system) in 36 patients with PKU (17.2 ± 10.1 years) and 18 healthy controls (17.9 ± 9.9 years). They reported significant differences in contrast sensitivity, colour vision, and electroretinography, mainly explained by the Phe /Tyr imbalance (dopamine hypothesis) rather than the LC-PUFA status [148]. Using optical coherence tomography (OCT) Nowak et al. reported a correlation in the retinal nerve fibre layer thickness and both lifetime blood Phe levels and IQ in 15 early treated patients with PKU (15.2 ± 5.2 years), although the mean thickness was similar to controls in other studies [149]. Servozo et al. reported lower thickness of parafoveal and perifoveal retinal layers and macular ganglion cell complex in 50 early treated adults with PKU (30.7 ± 8.0 years) compared to 50 controls (30.45 ± 7.18 years), using OCT angiography [150]. Finally, five adult patients who discontinued dietary treatment, were reported to have developed acute visual loss, which partly (n = 2) or completely (n = 3) resolved when dietary treatment was re-initiated [6,85]. Overall, there seems to be a retinal effect which might be a marker of neurological damage rather than impairment of the eye. However, a nutritional component, such as vitamin B12 deficiency, cannot be completely excluded. At this point, routine eye follow-up is not recommended. Recommendation 29* Issues with mental health and behavioural problems (i.e. concerns related to ageappropriate functioning in the community, at home, in education or the workplace) should be discussed as part of every clinical consultation and during neuropsychological assessments. Subjective or objective adaptive issues, emotional, behavioural or social concerns should prompt further exploration of difficulties (possibly with ad-hoc instruments such as validated questionnaires) and may include psychological referral. Brain MRI PKU is associated with white matter (WM) abnormalities and grey matter (GM) abnormalities on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). GM is responsible for processing and interpreting information, while WM is crucial for transmitting signals across different areas of the nervous system. However, due to the unclear clinical impact of WM and GM abnormalities, neuroimaging is not advocated in routine care. Therefore, this recommendation remains unchanged. Recent MRI Diffusion Weighted Imaging (DWI) studies confirm earlier findings and report reduced water diffusion in cerebral white matter and a negative correlation between DWI-related measures and blood and brain Phe levels [6,138,139]. Both reduction of whole and regional brain volumetry and swelling of cerebral areas have been reported in MRI studies [98,140-142], but their clinical significance is uncertain. A prospective study involving 37 early treated patients with PKU and 71 controls (7 to 21 years) undergoing neuropsychological and brain MRI assessments at 1.5-1.6-year time intervals detected a more rapid deterioration of DWI-derived markers with age in subjects with PKU than in controls. The authors propose the decline of mean diffusivity as the anatomical background of the effect of lifetime exposure to blood Phe on executive functions [141]. Published cases without WM abnormalities suggest the limited impact of blood Phe under 600 μmol/L on MRI WM signal [6]. Over this threshold, the severity of signal changes is influenced by lifetime and/or concurrent blood Phe although with large interindividual variability [6,78]. Recently, several papers have been published about arterial and cardiac function. HermidaAmeijeiras et al. evaluated pulse wave velocity as an arterial stiffness marker in 41 patients with PKU (aged 6 to 50 years) and matched 14 A.M.J. van Wegberg et al. Molecular Genetics and Metabolism 145 (2025) 109125 controls. They reported increased aortic stiffness in patients with PKU and an association with blood Phe levels. However, the PKU group included more obese patients than the control group and this may have explained the differences found [151]. Nonetheless, high blood Phe may be a risk factor for cardiac aging as suggested in a mouse study [152] and for reduction of thickness of ventricular wall and consequently reducing ventricular ejection capacity [153]. Currently there is insufficient data to support routine evaluation of heart function. in 5 caregivers reporting that their children with PKU were taking laxatives [133]. Issues such as abdominal pain, constipation, flatulence, retching and regurgitation have been associated with the high osmolality of the lower volume amino acid based protein substitutes [133,161]. It was first suggested in 2011 that the nutritional composition and characteristics of a Phe restricted diet might change the gut microbial ecology and affect host physiology [165]. Evidence suggests that gut microbiota is characterized by a lower microbial diversity [166,167] with potentially different taxonomic groups, which may impact the metabolomic profile. Verducci et al. described a lower degree of microbial diversity and a decrease in faecal butyrate content in patients with PKU [168], related with depletion of F. prausnitzii [169]. However, it is not clear if the presence of distinct taxonomic groups within the gut microbiome of patients with PKU is a consequence of the disease or its treatment [170]. More studies are needed to investigate the impact of pharmacological treatments and change in dietary practices or cGMP protein substitutes on microbiota in patients with PKU [171,172], and their influence on metabolomic profile [173]. 7.9.3. Kidney Although there are no reports of chronic renal failure in PKU, literature suggests some risk of renal glomerular dysfunction. Two large studies highlighted a higher adjusted prevalence ratio for renal insufficiency with hypertension and for chronic kidney disease compared to the general population, in patients with PKU in the USA and Germany, respectively [154,155]. These observational studies followed the report by Hennermann et al. who described in 67 patients with early and late diagnosed PKU aged 15-43 years that glomerular filtration rate decreased in 11/59 (19 %) in addition to proteinuria, defined as a protein excretion of >150 mg/24 h, in 19/62 patients (30.6 %). BMI was increased in 25 patients, while 10 patients did not adhere to the prescribed diet [156]. However, these results are in contrast to the finding of normal renal function markers and absence of arterial hypertension in 52 treated patients with PKU compared to controls [157]. They also found significantly lower plasma levels of asymmetric dimethylarginine (ADMA) when compared with controls, a finding partly confirmed by Andrade et al. [158]. ADMA is an endogenous inhibitor of nitric oxide synthase and is linked to kidney dysfunction [157]. Considering that renal response to protein/amino acid infusions is multifactorial [159] it is recommended that all evidence is carefully interpretated and all potential risk factors are considered. Commonly, studies do not describe renal function in patients with PKU and give limited dietary information, particularly about the type of protein substitutes prescribed and dosage of protein equivalent consumed. It is currently unclear if there is a negative impact of dietary treatment of PKU on renal function. Recommendation 32** Any kind of gastrointestinal symptoms can potentially be problematic and routine screening in the clinical setting may be considered. Bone Osteopenia and osteoporosis have been described in PKU for many years (van Wegberg 2017). Some studies describe a high rate of osteopenia (41 %) and osteoporosis (10 %) in adults with PKU [174] but recent metanalysis suggests that although bone density is lower than in normal population it remains within the normal range for the majority of patients [175]. Many factors have been implicated in the pathophysiology of low bone density observed in PKU, where an increase in osteoclast activity may have a central role [176,177]. Factors that have been suggested include inadequate calcium and vitamin D intakes [178,179], limited natural protein intake [6], energy deficiency [180,181], oxidative stress [177], fatty acid profile [182], and Phe-free protein substitutes. Patients with PKU have an increase in calcinuria, which is not usually associated with calcium deficiency [6]. Furthermore, the Phe-free amino acid supplements provide a higher dietary acid load, potentially increasing urinary excretion of renal net acid, calcium and magnesium [183]. Some studies have shown that male patients with PKU have a lower BMD than females [184]. A protective effect of cGMP has been proposed [6,185], but this was not confirmed by a 3-year longitudinal study in children [186]. Finally, no data is available evaluating if liberalization of a Phe-restricted diet with sapropterin treatment improves bone density [187]. Practically, good blood Phe control, an adequate intake of calcium and vitamin D, regular exercise and optimization of natural protein intake is important. We suggest follow-up of BMD during early adolescence which, if sub-optimal, can be improved before the peak bone mass is reached.

claims.source_text: A Phe-free/low Phe protein substitute should be prescribed to any patient with PKU treated with a Phe restricted diet consuming less than the FAO/WHO/UNU 2007 safe levels of natural protein intake. … Phe-free/low Phe protein substitutes should be evenly administered and given at least 3 times throughout the day. … Phe intake should be methodically titrated until blood Phe is consistently maintained within the Phe target range. If blood Phe levels are consistently maintained within therapeutic target range, a challenge with extra dietary Phe should be considered to avoid unnecessary restrictions. Phe deficiency should be avoided.

claims.claim: **Pegvaliase may be offered over 16 years of age** when sapropterin cannot achieve control, with close safety follow-up; it is not recommended in pregnancy or before conception.
claims.source_text: Patients with PKU >16 years of age who are not able to achieve metabolic control with pharmacological treatment with sapropterin dihydrochloride may be offered treatment with pegvaliase. • Due to the safety profile close follow-up with specific safety measures are required and must be clearly explained to patients. … the use of pegvaliase is currently not recommended during pregnancy or women in the pre-conception period.
claims.locator: van Wegberg AMJ, MacDonald A, Ahring K, et al., Molecular Genetics and Metabolism (Elsevier), 'European guidelines on diagnosis and treatment of phenylketonuria: First revision', vol. 145, article 109125, published 2025, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ymgme.2025.109125, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Late-diagnosed children and adolescents should always be treated;** in untreated adults, decide individually and try treatment for at least 6 months.
claims.source_text: In late-diagnosed children and adolescents with PKU, treatment should always be initiated, aiming to keep blood Phe levels within the recommended therapeutic target range. … In untreated adults with PKU, introduction of treatment can be beneficial in several domains, but an individual decision in the best interests of the patient should be taken. A treatment trial of at least 6 months should be considered to evaluate the effect.
claims.locator: van Wegberg AMJ, MacDonald A, Ahring K, et al., Molecular Genetics and Metabolism (Elsevier), 'European guidelines on diagnosis and treatment of phenylketonuria: First revision', vol. 145, article 109125, published 2025, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ymgme.2025.109125, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: 🚩 **Maternal PKU is a high-risk pregnancy:** high Phe is teratogenic (growth restriction, microcephaly, intellectual disability, congenital heart defects). Reach target Phe before conception; if already pregnant, within 7 days. Prevent unplanned pregnancy.
claims.source_text: Maternal PKU should be considered as a high-risk pregnancy, requiring counselling and the support of a multidisciplinary team to ensure good metabolic control and optimal outcome. … High blood Phe during pregnancy has a teratogenic effect on the developing foetus, causing growth retardation, microcephaly, intellectual disabilities, and birth defects, including congenital heart defects … The recommended therapeutic target Phe levels should be achieved pre-conception. If the patient is already pregnant on presentation, all measures should be taken to aim for therapeutic target Phe levels to be reached within 7 days. … Significant effort should be undertaken to avoid any unplanned pregnancies in women with PKU. Timely education and effective contraceptive methods are key elements.
claims.locator: van Wegberg AMJ, MacDonald A, Ahring K, et al., Molecular Genetics and Metabolism (Elsevier), 'European guidelines on diagnosis and treatment of phenylketonuria: First revision', vol. 145, article 109125, published 2025, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ymgme.2025.109125, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: 🚩 **Unplanned pregnancy: the metabolic centre contacts the woman the same day and diet starts within 24 h.**
claims.source_text: Women with unplanned pregnancy should be contacted by their metabolic centre the day of notification as rapid blood Phe reduction is essential. Dietary treatment should start immediately (within 24 h).
claims.locator: van Wegberg AMJ, MacDonald A, Ahring K, et al., Molecular Genetics and Metabolism (Elsevier), 'European guidelines on diagnosis and treatment of phenylketonuria: First revision', vol. 145, article 109125, published 2025, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ymgme.2025.109125, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **In pregnancy:** blood Phe at least twice weekly (weekly before conception); if Phe falls below 120 μmol/L, raise Phe intake by 50–100 mg/day at once; avoid weight loss. Give at least 400 μg folic acid daily before conception and for the first 12 weeks, and at least 200 mg/day DHA.
claims.source_text: Blood Phe should be monitored at least once weekly pre-conception and at least twice weekly during pregnancy. … Phe intake should be increased by 50-100 mg/day immediately when blood Phe is <120 μmol/L anytime during pregnancy. … Weight loss should be avoided in maternal PKU to avoid Phe toxicity particularly in the first trimester. … At least 400 μg of folic acid daily should be given to all women with PKU considering pregnancy and for the first 12 weeks of pregnancy … A daily intake of ≥200 mg/day of DHA (n-3) should be provided to all women with PKU who are considering pregnancy and during pregnancy.
claims.locator: van Wegberg AMJ, MacDonald A, Ahring K, et al., Molecular Genetics and Metabolism (Elsevier), 'European guidelines on diagnosis and treatment of phenylketonuria: First revision', vol. 145, article 109125, published 2025, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ymgme.2025.109125, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Fetal anomaly ultrasound at 18–22 weeks,** with extra growth scans if control is sub-optimal. Breastfeeding is supported whether or not the baby has PKU.
claims.source_text: Detailed follow-up by ultrasound with screening for organ development at 18-22 weeks is strongly recommended (similar to routine pregnancy management in most countries). If metabolic control is sub-optimal, then additional growth and development scans are strongly recommended. … In maternal PKU, breast-feeding infants either unaffected or affected by PKU is advocated.
claims.locator: van Wegberg AMJ, MacDonald A, Ahring K, et al., Molecular Genetics and Metabolism (Elsevier), 'European guidelines on diagnosis and treatment of phenylketonuria: First revision', vol. 145, article 109125, published 2025, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ymgme.2025.109125, retrieved 2026-09-23
